title: How are the mighty fallen (2 Samuel 1)
hookLine: David weeps for Saul, who hunted him, and for Jonathan
carry: swifter than eagles, stronger than lions

cards: A man runs into David's camp with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. He comes from the battle on Mount Gilboa, carrying a crown and a bracelet. Saul's.
The king is dead, he says, and Jonathan with him. Saul hunted David through caves and wilderness. Now the throne is open, and a man in David's position might feel relief.
Instead David takes hold of his own clothes and tears them, and so do all the men with him. They mourn, and weep, and fast until evening, for Saul, for Jonathan, and for the people. Then David sings.

teach.h: A LAMENT, WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF JASHER.
teach.b: The song is a lament, and the text says it is written in the book of Jasher. Its refrain, in the King James Bible: "The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!"
He doesn't want the news spread among the enemy: "Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon." He curses the mountains where they fell.

teach.h: DAVID PRAISES THE MAN WHO HUNTED HIM.
teach.b: And then he praises Saul. Not a word about the spears, the caves, the running. He tells the women of Israel to weep over Saul, who clothed them in scarlet.
He sings of the two together: "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions."
Some readers call it generous. Some call it political: a new king honoring the old one. The text doesn't settle it.
What it does is let David grieve the whole man, the king he was, not only the enemy he became.
Then the song turns personal: "I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful."

Two kinds of grief sit side by side: clean grief for a friend, and tangled grief for someone who did harm, and was also brave, and was also family. The refrain comes back at the end: how are the mighty fallen.
One song, big enough to hold both.

how: Some Christians read David's lament for Saul and Jonathan as a model of honest grief, and lines from it are sometimes read at funerals and memorials.

games.q: you're David. the king who hunted you is dead, and his crown is in front of you. what do you do first?
o: tear your clothes and mourn for him.
thank God for your enemy's defeat.
games.why: he tears his clothes, weeps, fasts until evening, and then sings a lament that praises Saul and Jonathan together.

practice: Let one person come to mind whose loss is tangled: someone who hurt you and also gave you something, or someone gone you never quite made peace with; if no one comes, choose someone whose life you're grieving while they're alive.
Don't tidy them up; let both be true, and find one honest good thing to say about them, as David did. If you pray, hold them before God without a verdict.
